blocks.title: Leaf-level hyperspectral detection and severity estimation of white rust in Indian mustard
blocks.subtitle: Detailed methodology for the 2025-26 ASD contact-probe leaf spectra – grouped, stratified 70:30 hold-out design – with the disease-research papers behind every step
lines: Animesh Panda · Ph.D. (Agricultural Physics) · ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi
Objective 1: spectral response and disease-specific features · Objective 2: machine-learning and deep-learning models
Methodology only: this document contains no results
Core reference: Ma et al. (2026), DT-EDNet for rice blast (IAENG International Journal of Applied Mathematics 56(11), 5380–5398), checked against the paper

blocks.text: How to read this document

This document describes, step by step, how the 2025-26 leaf spectra of white rust are analysed. It contains no results. Each step has a **method card** with the same rows, so that every step can be defended in the same way:

items: **What is done** – the operation in one or two sentences.
**Why at this position** – why the step comes here in the sequence and what it needs from earlier steps.
**Disease papers: what they did** – published plant-disease studies that used the same operation, and what exactly they did.
**How my step follows them** – which part is taken from the paper, and where and why this study differs.
**With my data (exact settings)** – the leaves used, the parameter values and the software.
**Output → next step** – what the step produces and which later step uses it.
**Alternatives and notes** – other options and the reason they were not chosen.
**Likely question → answer** – a short answer for the committee.

blocks.text: References are taken from plant-disease studies wherever such a study exists. Where an operation has no disease paper (for example the correction of detector steps), the original methods paper is cited and this is said openly. Chapter 9 collects all reference papers in one matrix, lists every departure from them with the reason, and gives the settings of every step in one table.

blocks.text: 1.2 Workflow

blocks.caption: Workflow of the methodology: experiment and quality control (A), the grouped 70:30 split (B), pre-processing and features (C), Objective 1 (D), Objective 2 (E), evaluation (F), covariate baseline (G), check of the validation design (H) and reproducibility (I).

blocks.text: The order matters. Quality control comes before everything. The 70:30 split is fixed before any feature is chosen or any model is fitted. Pre-processing works leaf by leaf, so it can be applied to all leaves. Objective 1 describes the disease on all leaves; when features are chosen for the models, the same chain is repeated on the training plots only (Step E2). The test plots are opened once, in Step F.

blocks.label: Data quality control decided in this methodology.
text: Two problems in the raw files are handled in Step A5 before any analysis: (1) **75 duplicated leaf spectra** – on 13 March 2026, in plots 13, 34, 38, 41 and 42, fifteen leaf columns were exact copies of other columns of the same plot; one copy of each is kept; (2) **a residual step at the 1000-nm detector join** of the ASD (between the VNIR and SWIR-1 detectors), which is removed by an additive correction (Hueni and Bialek, 2017) before smoothing and differentiation.
After quality control the data set has 2255 leaf spectra: 1571 in the 33 training plots and 684 in the 15 test plots (30.3%).

blocks.text: 2. Part A – Experiment, data collection and quality control

rows: 48 plots (5 m × 3.5 m) in a 48 m × 24 m field at IARI, New Delhi: one fungicide-sprayed healthy block (plots 1–12) and three unsprayed replications (R3 13–24, R2 25–36, R1 37–48). Each block holds the 12 combinations of three varieties (V1–V3) and four sowing dates (D1 9 Dec, D2 18 Dec, D3 27 Dec 2025, D4 9 Jan 2026). Infection is natural.
The design defines the units that later steps keep together (plots), the strata of the split (healthy vs unsprayed blocks) and the factors used to check robustness (variety, sowing date).

• Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): studied white rust of Indian mustard under natural infection over several seasons and sowing dates in India and related it to weather, to build forecasting models.
• Ram and Awasthi (2018): compared white rust in improved varieties of Indian mustard in the field by visual assessment.
• Mandal et al. (2023): field trial of rice genotypes under natural blast infection (upland and lowland) at Almora, scored on the 0–9 scale.

Natural field infection with several varieties and sowing dates, as in Chattopadhyay et al. (2011) and Mandal et al. (2023). A fungicide-sprayed block gives healthy leaves of the same age and variety (Saharan et al., 2014).
Plot plan in a1_prep.py (plot → block, timing, variety). Crop age at sampling (days after sowing, DAS) is the time variable because there is no inoculation date.
Plot table → A5 (labels), B1 (split by plots and blocks), F6 (strata), G (covariates).
Artificial inoculation (Mahlein et al., 2013; Lv et al., 2023) gives a known infection date but not field conditions; natural infection was chosen to match the UAV phase.
Why natural infection? → Because the models are meant for field conditions; the four sowing dates create crops of different ages under the same epidemic.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step A1: Field experiment and treatments.

rows: Leaf spectra with the ASD contact probe

On 11 and 24 February and 3 and 13 March 2026, leaves at three positions (L3 and L5: third and fifth fully expanded leaf from the top; LL: lowest green leaf) are measured in all 48 plots with an ASD FieldSpec spectroradiometer, contact probe and leaf clip (own halogen lamp), 350–2500 nm at 1 nm.
The leaf spectrum is the basic observation of every later step; the contact probe removes sun, sky, soil and atmosphere, so the spectrum contains only the leaf (Milton et al., 2009).

• Chen et al. (2023): measured tobacco leaves infected with TMV and PVY with an ASD FieldSpec 4 over 350–2500 nm.
• Martínez-Martínez et al. (2018): bean angular leaf spot; spectra measured in contact with the leaves estimated severity much better than spectra taken from above the crop.
• Meng et al. (2020): leaf reflectance of corn leaves with southern corn rust at several severity levels measured with a leaf clip, used to build disease indices.
• Baranowski et al. (2015): hyperspectral and thermal imaging of oilseed rape (~~Brassica napus~~) leaves responding to ~~Alternaria~~.
Same instrument class and the same single-leaf contact measurement as Chen et al. (2023) and Martínez-Martínez et al. (2018).
One Excel file per date; each leaf column has seven header rows (wavelength, plot, variety, growth stage, healthy/diseased, leaf level, score). 2339 leaf spectra recorded.
Raw spectra (X_leaf.npy) and leaf metadata → A5.
Why single leaves and not plot means? → The grade is given to each leaf, so leaf spectra and leaf grades match one to one; plot structure is respected in the split (B1).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step A2: Leaf spectra with the ASD contact probe.

rows: Visual severity grade of the same leaf
Each measured leaf is scored on the 0–9 white rust scale (grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9) immediately after measurement.
The grade is the reference (label) for all three tasks; it must belong to the same leaf as the spectrum.

• Mandal et al. (2023): rice blast scored on the 0–9 scale and related to spectra.
• Chen et al. (2023): tobacco virus severity in grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (GB/T 23222-2008) – the same six grades as here.
• Bock et al. (2010): reviewed visual severity assessment; raters disagree most between neighbouring classes.
Same 0–9 ordinal scale and the same six grade values as Chen et al. (2023); Bock et al. (2010) explains why ordinal metrics are used for Task B (F2).
Grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; diseased = grade > 0. After quality control: grade 0 552, 1 389, 3 409, 5 501, 7 278, 9 126 leaves.
Labels of Tasks A, B, C → A5, E1.
Image-based pustule area (Ashourloo et al., 2014; Lv et al., 2023) would reduce rater noise; not available for 2025-26.
Is a visual grade precise enough? → It is the field standard; its imprecision between neighbouring grades is expected (Bock et al., 2010) and is handled with ordinal metrics and a regression score.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step A3: Visual severity grade of the same leaf.

rows: Daily weather (IARI observatory, 1 Dec 2025 – 20 Mar 2026). For each sampling date: means of the 7 days ending the day before sampling (T max, T min, RH I, RH II, wind, sunshine, evaporation; rain as total); favourable days for leaf infection and staghead counted from each sowing date; crop age (DAS); growth-stage code; variety and sowing date.
These covariates describe the epidemic and form the sensor-free baseline of Step G, against which the spectra are judged.

• Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): defined the weather favourable to white rust of mustard: leaf infection at T max 16–24 °C, morning RH > 97% and afternoon RH > 40%; staghead at T max 20–29 °C, T min > 12 °C, morning RH > 97%.
• Bhattacharya and Chattopadhyay (2013): tracked mustard rot disease by combining surface meteorology with satellite remote sensing.
• Zhang et al. (2014a): forecast wheat powdery mildew from meteorological data with and without remote sensing.
The favourable-day counts use exactly the thresholds of Chattopadhyay et al. (2011); combining weather with sensor data follows Bhattacharya and Chattopadhyay (2013) and Zhang et al. (2014a).
7-day windows end the day before each date (no look-ahead); stage coded 1 vegetative, 2 flowering, 3 pod formation after the BBCH ranges (Lancashire et al., 1991).
One covariate row per leaf → G.
Why windows ending the day before? → So that no weather from after the measurement enters any model.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step A4: Weather and crop covariates.

rows: The four files are parsed into one leaf table and checked: (1) plots joined to the plan; (2) L4 spectra removed; (3) duplicated spectra removed; (4) residual detector step at 1000 nm corrected; (5) value checks.
Every later step assumes one correct spectrum per leaf. Duplicates would count the same leaf twice; a detector step creates a false feature in derivatives and wavelets.

• No disease paper describes these checks in detail; they follow the instrument literature.
• Hueni and Bialek (2017): showed that the joins between the three ASD detectors (near 1000 and 1800 nm) produce radiometric steps that change with instrument temperature, and gave an additive correction.
• Mandal et al. (2023) and Selvaprakash et al. (2026) report pre-processing of handheld spectroradiometer data before analysis.
The additive splice correction of Hueni and Bialek (2017) is applied; the same correction was used in my earlier white rust analyses that replicated Tian et al. (2021) and Mandal et al. (2023).

(1) Join each plot to block, timing and variety; check that the variety in the file equals the plot plan.
(2) Remove the 9 spectra labelled L4 (not a sampled position).
(3) Find identical spectra (all 2151 values equal) and keep one copy: 75 copies removed (13 March 2026; plots 13, 34, 38, 41, 42).
(4) Splice correction at each detector join (1000/1001 and 1800/1801 nm): the jump between the two bands is compared with the local slope on both sides; where the median excess is larger than 0.0005 reflectance, the bands above the join are shifted leaf by leaf so that the jump equals the local slope (needed at 1000 nm; no step at 1800 nm).
(5) Check grades (0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 only), 2151 bands, no missing values, reflectance range, all 48 plots on every date.
Result: 2255 leaf spectra.
meta.csv and corrected spectra → B1 (split), C (features).
Leaving the detector step in place would let ReliefF and wavelet selection pick the artefact (as found in my earlier Lv et al. (2023) replication).
How were duplicates found? → By comparing all 2151 values of every pair of spectra; identical spectra cannot come from two different leaves.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step A5: Data organisation and quality control.

rows: Task A: 0 = grade 0, 1 = grade > 0. Task B: six classes coded 0–5 for grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Task C: grade 0–9 as a number.
Each task answers a different practical question and needs its own metrics (F1–F3).

• Lv et al. (2023): asymptomatic and symptomatic detection plus severity classes for southern corn leaf blight.
• Chen et al. (2023): binary (healthy/infected) and six-class (severity grade) models for tobacco viruses.
• Zhang et al. (2012): normal / slight / heavy powdery mildew classes plus a PLSR estimate of the disease index.
• Mandal et al. (2023): regression and classification of rice blast severity on the 0–9 scale.
The combination of a detection task, a severity-class task and a severity regression follows Lv et al. (2023), Chen et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2012).
Class weights balanced in all classifiers because grade 9 is the rarest class (E3).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step A6: Labels for the three tasks.

blocks.text: 3. Part B – Validation design: the grouped, stratified 70:30 split
The split decides which leaves may teach the models and which leaves test them. It is fixed once, before any feature selection or model fitting, and is kept for every part of the analysis.

rows: Grouped, stratified 70:30 hold-out of whole plots
The 48 plots are divided once into 33 training plots (TRAIN) and 15 test plots (TEST). Whole plots go to one side only. Healthy and unsprayed plots are split separately.
It must come before Step C-E, because every choice that learns from the data (features, subsets, settings, epochs) may use only the training plots.

• Ma et al. (2026): rice blast (UAV hyperspectral, 2,690 canopy samples) divided by stratified sampling into training and test sets at 7:3, with 10% of the training set as validation; plus an independent cross-year test (2023 → 2024).
• Mandal et al. (2023): rice blast data divided by stratified sampling into two-thirds calibration and one-third validation; all modelling on the calibration part.
• Wang et al. (2016): wheat rust severity models checked with leave-one-out cross-validation and an external validation set.
• Kattenborn et al. (2022): plant mapping from UAV images; random splits over-estimated accuracy by up to 28% compared with spatially blocked splits.
• Roberts et al. (2017): showed that dependent samples must be held out in blocks.

The 70:30 proportion and stratification are those of Ma et al. (2026) and close to Mandal et al. (2023). Unlike them, whole plots are assigned, because leaves of one plot share soil, microclimate and inoculum (Roberts et al., 2017; Kattenborn et al., 2022).

(1) Plot table with block, timing, variety, number of leaves.
(2) Test plots per block type = round(0.30 × plots): 4 healthy, 11 unsprayed.
(3) Random candidates obeying the rules: the 11 unsprayed test plots are 11 different treatments, spread as evenly as possible over R1–R3, varieties and sowing dates; the 4 healthy test plots have different sowing dates.
(4) 5000 different candidates (seed 2026); each scored by |leaf share − 0.30| + 0.5 × (0.5 × Σ|grade-share difference| + 0.5 × Σ|date-share difference|).
(5) The lowest score is kept: test plots 1, 4, 5, 8 (healthy) and 13, 14, 18, 25, 27, 31, 35, 37, 44, 46, 48 (unsprayed).
After quality control: TRAIN 1571 leaves, TEST 684 leaves (30.3%). The split was drawn before quality control and is kept unchanged.
Column fold (0 = TEST, 1 = TRAIN) → every later step. Scripts split_lib.py, split_cfg.py.
Random leaf split (Ma et al., 2026; Mandal et al., 2023) is simpler but would put leaves of one plot on both sides; leave-one-replication-out tests every leaf once and is used as a check (H3).
Was the best of 5000 splits chosen because models did well on it? → No; the score uses only leaf, grade and date counts, never a spectrum or a model result. It is stratified sampling.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step B1: Grouped, stratified 70:30 hold-out of whole plots.

blocks.text: n_{test} is the number of leaves in the candidate test plots, N the number of all leaves, p_{g} the share of grade g and p_{d} the share of sampling date d. The first term keeps the test set at 30% of the leaves; the bracket keeps its grade and date mix like that of all leaves (Kuhn and Johnson, 2013).

blocks.caption: Field plan with the 15 test plots (dark), the 33 training plots (light) and the 11 training plots used for early stopping of the networks (purple).

rows: Settings, feature subsets and stopping epochs are chosen inside TRAIN with a second division by plot: inner GroupKFold(3) for machine learning (three rounds of 22 fitting and 11 scoring plots) and a fixed set of 11 validation plots for the networks.
A model must be tuned on data it is not tested on; tuning on TEST would make the test accuracy optimistic (Varma and Simon, 2006; Cawley and Talbot, 2010).

• Ma et al. (2026): 10% of the training set as validation; the model with the highest validation accuracy was kept and then tested once.
• Tian et al. (2021): rice leaf blast; SFFS wrapped around LDA, k-NN and SVM with 4-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times.
• Lv et al. (2023): southern corn leaf blight; RELIEF-F, SFFS and SVM with 4-fold stratified cross-validation repeated 100 times.
The inner validation of Ma et al. (2026), Tian et al. (2021) and Lv et al. (2023), but always by whole plots: GroupKFold(3) for ML and one third of the training plots for the networks.
ML: GroupKFold(3) over the 33 training plots. Networks: 11 training plots (6, 7, 11, 19, 24, 26, 28, 30, 36, 39, 41; random, seed 42) = 526 leaves; 22 plots = 1045 leaves fit the weights.
10% of the training leaves as in Ma et al. (2026) would be about three plots – too few to represent the blocks, and leaves of one plot would be in fitting and validation.
Why one third and not 10% for the networks? → With whole plots, a third (11 plots) covers all blocks; 10% would be about three plots.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step B2: Validation inside the training plots.

rows: Leakage rules that hold in every step

(1) Leaves of one plot are never on both sides of any division. (2) Every statistic that is learned (means and SDs for scaling, selected features, model weights) is computed from the fitting part only. (3) TEST is used once.
These rules make the test accuracy an honest estimate for new plots.

• Ambroise and McLachlan (2002): selecting features on all samples before validation gave error rates near zero even without real signal.
• Ma et al. (2026): feature selection and model training on the 2023 data, evaluation on the independent 2024 data.
• Roberts et al. (2017); Kattenborn et al. (2022): blocked validation for dependent samples.
Feature selection for the models is repeated on TRAIN (E2), as Ma et al. (2026) selected features on the training year only.
Scaling is fitted inside each inner fold (pipeline); the Objective 1 description (D) on all leaves is never passed to the models.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step B3: Leakage rules that hold in every step.

blocks.text: 4. Part C – Pre-processing and spectral features

Part C turns every corrected spectrum into the same set of numbers. Each operation works on one leaf at a time and learns nothing from other leaves, so it is applied to all leaves. Three families of features are produced: spectral bands and derivatives (C5–C6), indices including red-edge and continuum-removal features (C7–C9), and wavelet features (C10).

rows: Handling of the ASD detector joins

After the splice correction of Step A5, the two detector-join zones (990–1010 nm and 1790–1835 nm) are excluded from the candidate bands of Objective 1 and 2 feature selection; wavelet coefficients are excluded when their window (± 2 × scale) reaches a join zone; continuum-removal features whose window crosses a join are not used. Indices whose bands lie outside these zones are unaffected.

Even a small residual step at a join creates a sharp derivative and wavelet response that a selection method can mistake for a disease feature. Screening the zones before any selection removes that risk.

• No disease paper reports this check; it follows Hueni and Bialek (2017), who showed that ASD inter-detector steps vary with instrument temperature.
• In my replication of Lv et al. (2023) on these leaves, RELIEF-F ranked the 1800-nm step first in every task until the join zones were excluded; in my replication of Tian et al. (2021), two selected features lay on the joins (1005 and 1808 nm).
Correction (A5) plus exclusion of the join zones from selection, as in my earlier replications of Lv et al. (2023) and Tian et al. (2021).
Zones 990–1010 nm and 1790–1835 nm removed from Family 1 and Family 3 candidates; the spectra themselves are kept for the indices.
Do you lose information at 1000 and 1800 nm? → Only 66 nm of 2001 nm are excluded, and they carry instrument artefacts rather than leaf signal.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C1: Handling of the ASD detector joins.

rows: Each 1-nm spectrum (350–2500 nm) is smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter: second-order polynomial fitted in an 11-nm moving window.
Smoothing must come before the derivative (C5) and the wavelet transform (C10), which amplify random noise (Tsai and Philpot, 1998; Rinnan et al., 2009).

• Ma et al. (2026): all rice blast spectra were processed with Savitzky–Golay smoothing to reduce sensor noise before band selection.
• Selvaprakash et al. (2026): rice blast leaf spectra (350–2500 nm) pre-processed with Savitzky–Golay smoothing, followed by SNV and MSC, before the band-pair index search.
• Chen et al. (2023): Savitzky–Golay smoothing of ASD tobacco leaf spectra (350–2500 nm) gave the best SVM model of TMV and PVY severity among the pre-processing options tested.
• Mandal et al. (2023): Savitzky–Golay smoothing of rice blast spectra before index and band analysis.
Same filter as all four disease studies; window 11 nm and order 2 (Savitzky and Golay, 1964).
scipy.signal.savgol_filter(window 11, polyorder 2) on 350–2500 nm before trimming (C3), so the filter has full support at 400 and 2400 nm.

SNV and MSC (Selvaprakash et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2023) remove scatter differences but change the absolute reflectance needed by published indices; the contact probe already standardises illumination, so they are not used.
Why 11 nm? → It suppresses detector noise while keeping the red-edge shape; a window of 11 points with order 2 is a common choice in leaf-spectra studies (Selvaprakash et al., 2026).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C2: Savitzky–Golay smoothing.

rows: After smoothing, the spectrum is trimmed to 400–2400 nm; 350–399 nm and 2401–2500 nm are discarded.
The detector ends have low signal and high noise; trimming after smoothing avoids edge effects of the filter.

• Meng et al. (2020): southern corn rust leaf spectra trimmed at the noisy ends to 400–2450 nm before building disease indices.
• Matzrafi et al. (2017): leaf spectra measured with an ASD FieldSpec 4 and contact probe; the noisy edges were removed and the range set to 400–2400 nm.
• Chen et al. (2025): ASD FieldSpec 4 leaf spectra trimmed to 400–2400 nm because of noise at the extreme wavelengths.
Same range as Matzrafi et al. (2017) and Chen et al. (2025) with the same instrument and the same reason; Meng et al. (2020) is the disease study with the same practice.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C3: Spectral range 400–2400 nm.

rows: The water-absorption regions (about 1350–1460 nm and 1790–1960 nm) are kept, except the join zone 1790–1835 nm screened in C1.
With a contact probe and its own lamp the light path is a few millimetres of leaf, so these regions measure leaf water, which white rust reduces in infected tissue (Mishra et al., 2009).

• Chen et al. (2023) and Selvaprakash et al. (2026): full 350–2500 nm leaf spectra including the water regions.
• Apan et al. (2004): sugarcane orange rust detected with disease–water stress indices (DWSI) that use SWIR water-sensitive bands.
• Mandal et al. (2023): removed the water bands because their spectra were affected by atmospheric water vapour – not the case for a contact probe.
Leaf-level studies with their own light keep the full range; the reason Mandal et al. (2023) removed the bands (atmosphere) does not apply.
Water regions enter Families 1–3 and the water and DWSI indices (C7).
Why not remove the water bands as many papers do? → Those papers measured through air under sunlight; the contact probe has no atmospheric path.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C4: Water-absorption bands kept.

rows: The first derivative of each smoothed spectrum is computed with the same Savitzky–Golay filter (window 11, order 2, derivative 1), in units of reflectance per nm.
The derivative removes additive offsets between leaves (thickness, surface, probe contact) and turns the red edge into a peak whose height and position can be measured.

• Zhang et al. (2012): wheat powdery mildew; derivative spectral features (amplitude, position and area of the blue, yellow and red edges) among 32 spectral features for PLSR and Fisher discriminant analysis.
• Lv et al. (2023): first-order spectral derivatives at every band were one of four spectral enhancements; adding them improved severity classification of southern corn leaf blight most.
• Anuar et al. (2017): Ganoderma in oil palm seedlings; first-derivative analysis for de-noising before index development.
• Martínez-Martínez et al. (2018): bean angular leaf spot; raw and first-derivative reflectance compared for severity estimation.

First derivatives at every band, as in Lv et al. (2023), and derivative red-edge features (C8), as in Zhang et al. (2012). The second derivative is not used because it amplifies noise (Tsai and Philpot, 1998).
scipy.signal.savgol_filter(window 11, polyorder 2, deriv 1) on 350–2500 nm, then trimmed to 400–2400 nm.
Derivative spectra at 1 nm → C6 (5-nm bands), C8 (red-edge parameters).
Simple differences between neighbouring bands are avoided because they lower the signal-to-noise ratio (Rinnan et al., 2009).
Why the derivative at all? → It is the standard way to remove baseline differences and sharpen the red edge (Demetriades-Shah et al., 1990; Tsai and Philpot, 1998).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C5: First derivative (no second derivative).

rows: For the band-based searches (NDSI/RSI maps, effective ranges, SHAP-CARS candidates), reflectance and first-derivative spectra are reduced to 5-nm bands: each band is the mean of the five 1-nm values centred on it (λ − 2 … λ + 2 nm), for λ = 400, 405 … 2400 nm.

Neighbouring 1-nm values are almost identical (the ASD records at 1.4–2 nm steps with about 3–10 nm resolution and interpolates to 1 nm), so the exhaustive searches of Step D run on 5-nm bands without losing spectral shape. Indices and red-edge parameters still use the 1-nm spectra.

• Ma et al. (2026): used a reduced sampling of the spectrum to compute the R² contour maps of NDSI and RSI against rice blast severity, from which the effective wavelength ranges were taken.
• Mandal et al. (2023): resampled the 1-nm rice blast spectra to 10-nm bands by averaging before band selection and the two-band index search.
• Mahlein et al. (2013): worked at about 6-nm spectral resolution and kept selected wavelengths at least 50 nm apart because neighbouring wavelengths are highly correlated.
Band averaging as in Mandal et al. (2023), at a finer 5-nm interval; reduced sampling for the band-pair maps as in Ma et al. (2026).
401 reflectance bands (R400 … R2400) and 401 derivative bands (FD400 … FD2400), minus the join zones of C1.
Using every 1-nm band (Lv et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2021) gives 2001 nearly identical bands per type; those studies then merged features less than 10 nm apart, which has a similar effect.

Why 5 nm and not 1 nm? → 1-nm values are interpolated and redundant; 5-nm averaging follows the band averaging of Mandal et al. (2023) and the reduced sampling of Ma et al. (2026), while indices and the red-edge position keep 1-nm precision.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C6: Band features on a 5-nm grid.

rows: 41 published indices are computed for every leaf from the smoothed 1-nm reflectance: greenness and structure, pigment, red-edge, water and disease indices (Appendix A).
Indices summarise physiology in a form that can be compared with other studies and transferred to other sensors; they are Family 2 of the feature selection.

• Mandal et al. (2023): 26 published indices evaluated against rice blast severity, plus two new blast indices (RBI and NDBI from R1148 and R1301).
• Ma et al. (2026): a set of common vegetation indices (including PSSRb, SR, GNDVI, RVI, RVSI, WBI) computed for rice blast.
• Zhang et al. (2012): 11 hyperspectral vegetation indices among the spectral features of wheat powdery mildew.
• Mahlein et al. (2013): the Healthy Index (HI) for sugar-beet diseases; Apan et al. (2004): disease–water stress indices (DWSI) for sugarcane orange rust.
The index set contains the indices used in these disease studies (HI, DWSI-1 to 5, RVSI, PRI, ARI, PSRI, NDVI family, water indices) plus the rice blast indices RBI and NDBI of Mandal et al. (2023).
Formulas and original references in Appendix A; all computed at 1 nm.
Index table (41 columns) → C8 (adds REP, Dr, REarea), D6 (adds data-driven indices), D7.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C7: Published vegetation and disease indices.

rows: From the 1-nm first derivative between 680 and 760 nm: red-edge position REP (wavelength of the largest derivative), Dr (that largest derivative) and REarea (sum of the derivative over 680–760 nm).
Chlorophyll loss moves the red edge to shorter wavelengths and lowers its slope (Horler et al., 1983; Filella and Peñuelas, 1994).

• Zhang et al. (2012): red-edge amplitude (Dr), red-edge position (λr) and red-edge area (SDr) of wheat leaves with powdery mildew.
• Mandal et al. (2023): REP, red-edge amplitude and area from the first derivative of rice blast spectra.
Same three parameters (Dr, REP, area) as Zhang et al. (2012) and Mandal et al. (2023), computed at 1 nm.
REP = 680 + index of the maximum derivative in 680–760 nm; Dr in 10^{−3} nm^{−1}; REarea in reflectance units.
Three parameters added to the index table → D6, D7.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C8: Red-edge parameters.

rows: The continuum (convex hull) is removed over the chlorophyll absorption feature (530–760 nm) and the leaf-water features near 1200, 1450 and 1940 nm; for each feature the depth, width (at half depth), area and position are computed. The 970-nm water feature is not used because its window crosses the 1000-nm detector join.
Continuum removal isolates the shape of an absorption feature from the overall brightness of the leaf (Clark and Roush, 1984; Kokaly and Clark, 1999).

• Zhang et al. (2012): depth, width and area of the 550–750 nm continuum-removed absorption feature among the spectral features of wheat powdery mildew.
• In my earlier combined-feature analysis of these leaves (Mandal et al. (2023) workflow), continuum-removal features were among the features chosen by GA-PLS.
The 550–750 nm depth, width and area exactly as in Zhang et al. (2012); the water features follow the band-depth analysis of Kokaly and Clark (1999).
Continuum = upper convex hull of the 1-nm reflectance between the feature shoulders; features overlapping a join zone (C1) are not used.
Continuum-removal features added to Family 2 → D7.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C9: Continuum-removal absorption features.

rows: The continuous wavelet transform (Mexican-hat mother wavelet) is applied to each smoothed 1-nm spectrum at dyadic scales 2^{1} to 2^{6}; every coefficient WF(λ, scale) is a candidate feature (Family 3).
Low scales capture narrow absorption features and high scales the broad shape, so wavelet features describe changes that bands and indices miss (Cheng et al., 2010).

• Tian et al. (2021): rice leaf blast from asymptomatic to mild stages; wavelet features outperformed reflectance bands and spectral indices.
• Lv et al. (2023): wavelet features were one of four spectral enhancements for southern corn leaf blight and the best single feature type.
• Zhang et al. (2014b): wheat yellow rust at leaf level; wavelet features estimated severity better than conventional features, including derivative features.

Mexican-hat continuous wavelet analysis as in Tian et al. (2021), Lv et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2014b). In my replications of Tian et al. (2021) and Lv et al. (2023) on these leaves, wavelet features were the best single feature type.
pywt.cwt(mexh) on 400–2400 nm after splice correction; scales 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64; join zones excluded (C1).

Why add wavelet features if DT-EDNet did not use them? → Ma et al. (2026) used image texture as a third feature family; texture does not exist for single-leaf spectra, and wavelet features play that role for spectra (Tian et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2023).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step C10: Continuous wavelet features.

blocks.text: 5. Part D – Objective 1: spectral response and the disease-specific feature set

Part D describes how white rust changes the leaf spectrum and which compact set of features describes it. It follows the feature-selection chain of the DT-EDNet study (Ma et al., 2026) – effective wavelength ranges from band-pair maps, optimal wavelengths by SHAP-CARS, vegetation indices – and adds the steps of the leaf-level disease studies that worked best on these data in my earlier analyses: ReliefF ranking (Mahlein et al., 2013; Lv et al., 2023), wavelet features with region representatives (Tian et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2023) and the variance inflation factor (Lv et al., 2023). Run on all leaves, Part D is a description; for the models the same chain is repeated on the training plots only (Step E2).

blocks.caption: Feature-selection chain of Objective 1 and Step E2: three feature families, their selection steps, the VIF step and the use of the disease-specific feature set by the models.

rows: Mean spectra by grade and difference from healthy leaves
Mean ± SD reflectance and first derivative of each grade over 400–2400 nm; difference spectrum of each grade from grade 0.
The first, model-free evidence of where and in which direction the spectrum changes; it guides the interpretation of every selected feature.

• Mandal et al. (2023): mean and SD spectra of each rice blast severity level and difference from healthy plants.
• Mahlein et al. (2010): spectral difference and reflectance sensitivity of sugar-beet leaves with three diseases at each wavelength.
• Zhang et al. (2012): mean reflectance of normal, slight and heavy powdery mildew leaves.
• Shukla et al. (2024): reflectance of aphid-infested and healthy mustard measured with ground spectroscopy.
Mean, SD and difference-from-healthy spectra as in Mandal et al. (2023); for mustard, Shukla et al. (2024) is the closest crop study.
All 2255 leaves; 5-nm bands; healthy reference = grade 0.
Spectral regions of change → interpretation of D4–D12.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D1: Mean spectra by grade and difference from healthy leaves.

rows: Pearson r between the grade and each 5-nm reflectance and derivative band.
Shows the strength and sign of the relationship at every wavelength; used to read the band-pair maps and the selected bands.

• Zhang et al. (2012): correlation of each spectral feature with the powdery mildew disease index, ranked by R².
• Mandal et al. (2023): correlation of indices and bands with rice blast severity.
All leaves; reflectance and derivative separately.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D2: Correlation spectra.

rows: Spectra by growth stage and by factor
Mean spectra of each grade within each growth stage; mean grade by stage, variety, leaf position and sowing date.
Growth stage and date change the leaf spectrum independently of disease; the check shows whether the disease signal holds within each stage.

• Lv et al. (2023): spectra of healthy and infected corn leaves compared stage by stage (asymptomatic, symptomatic).
• Tian et al. (2021): rice leaf blast spectra analysed separately for the asymptomatic, early and mild stages.
Stage-wise comparison as in Lv et al. (2023) and Tian et al. (2021).
Stages vegetative, flowering, pod formation; four sowing dates; three leaf positions; three varieties.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D3: Spectra by growth stage and by factor.

rows: NDSI and RSI R² maps and effective wavelength ranges

For every pair of 5-nm reflectance bands (i < j), NDSI = (R_{i} − R_{j})/(R_{i} + R_{j}) and RSI = R_{i}/R_{j} are computed and their R² with the grade drawn as maps. Bands taking part in pairs with R² ≥ 0.5 form the effective ranges; if no pair reaches 0.5, the pairs in the top 5% of R² are used.
The maps show which band combinations follow the disease and restrict the candidate bands of SHAP-CARS to the informative regions.

• Ma et al. (2026): R² contour maps of NDSI and RSI against rice blast severity (450–1000 nm, reduced sampling); the effective ranges were the regions where R² of both indices exceeded 0.5 (455–503, 520–661 and 702–1000 nm).
• Tian et al. (2021): kept the top 5% of features by separability when choosing disease-sensitive features of rice leaf blast.
• Mandal et al. (2023): searched all two-band ratio and normalised-difference combinations against rice blast severity.
Maps, indices and the 0.5 threshold exactly as Ma et al. (2026); the top-5% fall-back follows Tian et al. (2021) and is needed because single-leaf spectra correlate more weakly than canopy spectra.
About 80 000 band pairs of 5-nm reflectance over 400–2400 nm (join zones excluded); R² from the squared Pearson r with the grade.
Effective ranges → D5 candidates; best NDSI and RSI pair → D6.
Why a fall-back to the top 5%? → R² ≥ 0.5 was set for canopy images; for single leaves no pair may reach it, and the top-5% rule of Tian et al. (2021) keeps the most informative pairs.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D4: NDSI and RSI R² maps and effective wavelength ranges.

rows: Candidates: reflectance and derivative bands inside the effective ranges, plus red-edge derivatives 680–760 nm. (1) An XGBoost model predicts the grade; bands are ranked by mean |SHAP|, and the top 40% are kept. (2) Monte Carlo cross-validation chooses the number of PLS components. (3) CARS is run 20 times; bands chosen in at least half of the runs (at most 15) are the optimal wavelengths (OW).
Hundreds of correlated bands cannot be given directly to a model; SHAP removes uninformative bands first, so that CARS works on a smaller, relevant set (Ma et al., 2026).

• Ma et al. (2026): SHAP-CARS – SHAP values of an ensemble model ranked the bands, Monte Carlo cross-validation chose the number of PLS components, and CARS eliminated redundant variables over many iterations; 12 key wavelengths were kept for rice blast.
• CARS for disease bands: pine wilt disease and cotton Verticillium wilt studies used CARS to select characteristic bands from ASD spectra.
• Li et al. (2009): introduced CARS (PLS coefficients as weights, exponentially decreasing number of bands, adaptive reweighted sampling).
The three stages of Ma et al. (2026) in the same order. Two additions: CARS is repeated 20 times with a 50% stability rule, and the Monte Carlo splits are made by plot.
XGBoost 300 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.05, subsample 0.8; MCCV 50 random 80/20 divisions by plot, 1–15 PLS components; CARS 50 iterations per run; seeds 42 + run.

RFE-SHAP and SAND were the two other selectors of Ma et al. (2026); SHAP-CARS was kept because it gave the most compact subset in that study and combines a non-linear ranking with a PLS-based elimination.
Why repeat CARS 20 times? → CARS depends on random sampling; keeping bands chosen in at least half of the runs makes the selection reproducible.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D5: Optimal wavelengths by SHAP-CARS.

rows: Data-driven indices: best NDSI, best RSI and the White Rust Index

The best NDSI and RSI pairs of D4 (bands at least 10 nm apart) are added as indices. The White Rust Index WRI = NDSI(λ1, λ2) + w·R_{λ3} is searched over the 200 best NDSI pairs (bands at least 50 nm apart), every λ3 at 10-nm steps and w ∈ {−1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1}, scored by |r| with the grade.
A data-driven index captures the white rust signal of these leaves; the third band can correct an effect that a two-band index cannot (Mahlein et al., 2013).

• Mahlein et al. (2013): spectral disease indices for sugar-beet diseases built as a normalised difference of two wavelengths plus or minus a third wavelength; selected wavelengths at least 50 nm apart.
• Mandal et al. (2023): new rice blast indices from the best two-band combination (RBI = R1148/R1301; NDBI from the same bands).
• Selvaprakash et al. (2026): searched more than one million normalised-difference pairs for rice blast and proposed RBI = (R1068 − R1560)/(R1068 + R1560).
• Ma et al. (2026): best NDSI and RSI from the band-pair maps.
The WRI form and the 50-nm rule are those of Mahlein et al. (2013); the exhaustive pair search follows Mandal et al. (2023) and Selvaprakash et al. (2026).
Searches on 5-nm reflectance; WRI values computed from 1-nm reflectance at the chosen wavelengths.
NDSI_best, RSI_best and WRI added to Family 2 → D7.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D6: Data-driven indices: best NDSI, best RSI and the White Rust Index.

rows: Among Family 2 (published indices, red-edge parameters, continuum-removal features, data-driven indices), features correlated at |r| ≥ 0.95 form clusters; from each cluster the feature most correlated with the grade is kept.
Many indices are near-copies (NDVI family, simple ratios); ReliefF ranks are unreliable among near-identical features.

• Ma et al. (2026): correlation analysis among the vegetation indices to judge which indices were redundant and which carried independent information.
• Tian et al. (2021) and Lv et al. (2023): kept one representative of features that described the same region or property.
Correlation-based redundancy screening as in Ma et al. (2026), with an explicit |r| ≥ 0.95 cut-off.
Pearson r among all Family 2 features; threshold 0.95.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D7: Redundancy filter of the indices.

rows: ReliefF / RReliefF ranking of the indices
The remaining indices are ranked with ReliefF for detection and six grades and with RReliefF for the score; the top five per task are the selected indices (VI).
ReliefF rewards features that separate classes among similar leaves and can reward a feature that is useful together with others (Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003).

• Mahlein et al. (2013): RELIEF-F selected the most relevant wavelengths and wavelength differences for the sugar-beet disease indices.
• Lv et al. (2023): RELIEF-F with 10 nearest hits and misses ranked bands, indices, derivatives and wavelet features of southern corn leaf blight before SFFS.
ReliefF with k = 10 neighbours as in Lv et al. (2023). Added: neighbours from the same plot are excluded, so plot similarity cannot raise the weights.
Features min–max scaled; k = 10; ReliefF (classes) or RReliefF (score); top 5 per task.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D8: ReliefF / RReliefF ranking of the indices.

rows: Wavelet-feature screening by separability and regions

For each wavelet coefficient, separability is measured (detection: best balanced accuracy of a single threshold between healthy and diseased leaves; grades and score: |r| with the grade). The top 5% are kept; coefficients of the same scale less than 10 nm apart are merged into a region, and the region representative is the coefficient with the highest separability. The representatives are ranked with ReliefF/RReliefF and the top five per task form WF.
There are about 12 000 wavelet coefficients; screening, merging and ranking reduce them to a few non-redundant features.

• Tian et al. (2021): separability of bands, wavelet coefficients and indices by thresholding; top 5% kept; features common to all dates merged into regions with one representative; then SFFS.
• Lv et al. (2023): RELIEF-F ranking of wavelet features; features within 10 nm of a better one at the same scale dropped.
Thresholding separability, top 5% and region representatives as in Tian et al. (2021); the 10-nm merging and ReliefF ranking as in Lv et al. (2023).
Mexican-hat coefficients of C10; join zones excluded; top 5 representatives per task.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D9: Wavelet-feature screening by separability and regions.

rows: Variance inflation factor and the disease-specific feature set

For each task, OW + VI + WF are pooled; the feature with the largest variance inflation factor is removed one at a time until all VIF < 10. The remaining features are the disease-specific feature set (DSF) of that task.
Optimal wavelengths, indices and wavelet features overlap; strongly collinear inputs make models unstable and explanations unreliable.

• Lv et al. (2023): VIF < 10 within each feature type before SFFS for southern corn leaf blight.
• O'Brien (2007) and Dormann et al. (2013): VIF of 10 as the usual limit and methods for collinear predictors.
The VIF < 10 rule of Lv et al. (2023), applied to the pooled families.
VIF_{j} = 1/(1 − R_{j}^{2}), with R_{j}^{2} from regressing feature j on all others; iterative removal.
DSF of Tasks A, B and C → D11, E2, E4, E6.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D10: Variance inflation factor and the disease-specific feature set.

rows: The Jeffries–Matusita (JM) distance between every pair of grades is computed on the DSF of Task B.
It shows, before any classifier, which grades the selected features can separate and which overlap.

• Mandal et al. (2023): JM distance between rice blast severity levels; almost all levels were separable (JM > 1.92) except levels 4 and 5.
• Das et al. (2020): JM distance as one tier of a four-tier hierarchy (statistical test, feature selection, separability, classification) for rice genotypes with field spectroradiometry.
JM distance on the selected features as in Mandal et al. (2023) and Das et al. (2020).
JM = 2(1 − e^{−B}) with the Bhattacharyya distance B under Gaussian class distributions (Richards, 2013); all 15 grade pairs.
Separability table → interpretation of Task B (F2).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D11: Separability of the grades (Jeffries–Matusita distance).

rows: Principal component analysis of the 5-nm reflectance; scores of the first components plotted with 95% ellipses of each grade.
Shows the main structure of the data and whether grades form separate or overlapping groups.

• Selvaprakash et al. (2026): PCA of rice blast leaf spectra; most of the variance in five components.
• Martínez-Martínez et al. (2018): PCA of bean leaf spectra before neural-network severity estimation.
• Shukla et al. (2024): PCA loadings to identify key bands of aphid-infested mustard.
Exploratory PCA as in Selvaprakash et al. (2026) and Shukla et al. (2024).
Visual check of grade overlap → discussion.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step D12: Principal component analysis.

blocks.text: 6. Part E – Objective 2: machine-learning and deep-learning models

rows: Ten model types are trained for each of the three tasks: SVM/SVR, random forest, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours and PLS-DA/PLSR (machine learning), and DNN-F1, DT-EDNet, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18 and ConvNeXt V2-Atto (deep learning).
Comparing classical and deep models on the same features and the same split shows whether the disease signal needs a deep network.

• Ma et al. (2026): DT-EDNet compared with EfficientNet, ResNet18 and ConvNeXt V2 under identical settings for rice blast.
• Tian et al. (2021): LDA, k-NN and SVM wrapped in SFFS for rice leaf blast.
• Mandal et al. (2023): PLS, random forest, MARS and SVM for rice blast severity.
• Chen et al. (2023): SVM and random forest for tobacco virus severity; Gold et al. (2020): PLS-DA for potato late and early blight.
The four networks of Ma et al. (2026) and the classical models used in the leaf-level disease studies.
15 machine-learning and 15 deep-learning models (5 types × 3 tasks each).
blocks.caption: Method card – Step E1: Model matrix.

rows: Feature selection repeated on the training plots
The whole chain of Part D (D4–D10) is run again on the training plots only; its DSF of each task is the only input of the models.
Features chosen with the test plots would make the test accuracy optimistic (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002).

• Ma et al. (2026): feature selection and model training on the 2023 data; testing on the independent 2024 data.
• Mandal et al. (2023): all selection and calibration on the calibration set; validation set kept apart.
Selection on the training part only, as in Ma et al. (2026) and Mandal et al. (2023).
Same settings as D4–D10 on the 1571 training leaves; index values of the test leaves are computed with the wavelengths chosen on TRAIN.
DSF of Tasks A, B, C (training plots) → E3–E7.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step E2: Feature selection repeated on the training plots.

rows: Features are standardised with the mean and SD of the fitting part (inside each inner fold, then of all training plots for the final model). Classifiers use balanced class weights.
Scale-sensitive models (SVM, k-NN, PLS, networks) need comparable features; class weights stop the model from ignoring grade 9.

• Lv et al. (2023): standardised inputs and balanced classes for SVM.
• Ma et al. (2026): cross-entropy loss with label smoothing 0.01 for the networks; the same smoothing is used here, with class weights added because the grades are unequal.
Standardisation and balancing as in Lv et al. (2023).
scikit-learn Pipeline(StandardScaler, model); class_weight = balanced (XGBoost: balanced sample weights); networks: inverse-frequency class weights in the cross-entropy loss.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step E3: Scaling and class weights.

rows: For each machine-learning model, SFFS adds the feature that most improves the mean inner-fold score and after each addition tries to remove one; the best subset of every size up to 15 is recorded, and the smallest subset within 1% of the best inner score is kept.
Each model may need a different, smaller subset of the DSF; a wrapper choice gives the optimal feature combination for that model.

• Tian et al. (2021): SFFS wrapped around LDA, k-NN and SVM found optimal feature combinations of 2–4 features for rice leaf blast; SVM-SFFS was best.
• Lv et al. (2023): SFFS with the SVM macro-F1 as criterion after RELIEF-F and VIF for southern corn leaf blight.
SFFS as in Tian et al. (2021) with the macro-F1 criterion of Lv et al. (2023); the 1% rule follows the one-standard-error idea of Hastie et al. (2009).
mlxtend SFFS; criterion macro-F1 (A, B) or negative RMSE (C); inner GroupKFold(3) by plot.
Feature subset of each model → E5.
Why the smallest subset within 1%? → Neighbouring subset sizes differ by less than their noise; the smaller subset generalises better.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step E4: Sequential floating forward selection (SFFS).

rows: Grid search and final fit of the machine-learning models
On the SFFS subset, the grid of each model is searched with the same inner folds; the best setting is refitted on all training plots and predicts the test leaves once.
Hyper-parameters are chosen without the test plots; the refitted model is the delivered model.

• Tian et al. (2021): SVM C and γ chosen by grid search for each comparison.
• Lv et al. (2023): SVM C and γ by grid search with cross-validation.
Grid search inside the training part as in Tian et al. (2021) and Lv et al. (2023), by plot.
15 machine-learning models and their test predictions → F.
blocks.caption: Method card – Step E5: Grid search and final fit of the machine-learning models.

rows: DNN-F1 (dense network on the feature vector) and four image networks fed with a k × k pseudo-image of the DSF: DT-EDNet, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18, ConvNeXt V2-Atto.
DT-EDNet is the network of the core reference paper; the three others are its comparison networks.

• Ma et al. (2026): DT-EDNet – 3 × 3 convolutional embedding (128 channels) → squeeze-and-excitation → dual transformer group (one kernel transformer block with CBAM and four token transformer blocks, 4 attention heads) → class token, LayerNorm, linear head; the input spectral vector was reshaped into a pseudo-2D representation; AdamW (learning rate 6 × 10^{−4}, weight decay 10^{−5}), cosine schedule to 10^{−6} over 300 epochs, batch 32, label smoothing 0.01, gradient clipping 1.2, dropout 0.03, seed 42, early stopping with patience 60 and minimum improvement 5 × 10^{−5}; the model with the best validation accuracy was kept; all comparison networks used identical settings.
• Sharma et al. (2019): DeepInsight – turning non-image data into images for convolutional networks.

Architecture and optimiser settings exactly as Ma et al. (2026). Adapted: at most 100 epochs with patience 20 (the same patience-to-epochs ratio of 0.2 as 60/300), validation on 11 training plots, model selection by validation macro-F1 (A, B) or RMSE (C) because the classes are unequal; stride-1 stems so the small pseudo-image is not reduced away.
Pseudo-image side k = max(3, ⌈√p⌉) for p features, unused cells zero; PyTorch; fit on 1045 leaves of 22 plots, early stopping on 526 leaves of 11 plots; the best-epoch network is the delivered model.
15 networks and their test predictions → F.
300 epochs with patience 60 on CPU is not practical for 15 networks plus configurations and ablation; the shorter schedule keeps the same ratio.
Is a 4 × 4 pseudo-image meaningful? → It is an arrangement of features, not a picture (Sharma et al., 2019); this is tested directly by comparing with DNN-F1 and the machine-learning models.

Shows which feature family the networks use best and whether each DT-EDNet module contributes.
• Ma et al. (2026): compared feature configurations (spectral bands, vegetation indices, texture indices and their fusion) and removed DT-EDNet modules one at a time.

blocks.text: 7. Part F – Evaluation on the test plots
Every model of Part E predicts the 684 test leaves once. Nothing is changed after this step.

rows: Confusion matrix → overall accuracy (OA), Cohen's kappa, macro-F1, sensitivity (recall of diseased leaves), specificity (recall of healthy leaves), precision; area under the ROC curve (AUC) from the predicted probability or decision value.
OA alone hides which error a model makes; macro-F1 treats the healthy and diseased classes equally although healthy leaves are fewer; AUC does not depend on one decision threshold.

• Ma et al. (2026): OA, Cohen's kappa, macro-average recall, macro-average F1, per-class precision/recall/F1 and specificity on the test set.
• Selvaprakash et al. (2026): F1, kappa and AUC of rice blast indices.

blocks.text: 10. Likely questions and answers

blocks.a: It is the proportion used in the core reference paper (Ma et al., 2026: stratified 7:3) and close to the two-thirds : one-third of Mandal et al. (2023); a 20–30% test share is the usual rule (Gholamy et al., 2018). It leaves 15 test plots, enough for a plot bootstrap.

blocks.q: Why split by plots and not by leaves as Ma et al. (2026) did?
blocks.a: Ma et al. split canopy samples at random; here many leaves come from each plot and share its conditions. Random leaf splits would put near-copies in training and test (Roberts et al., 2017; Kattenborn et al., 2022). Step H2 measures that inflation directly.

blocks.q: Where is the reference for taking 5-nm bands?
blocks.a: Ma et al. (2026) used a reduced sampling of the spectrum for the NDSI/RSI maps; Mandal et al. (2023) averaged 1-nm spectra into 10-nm bands before band selection; Mahlein et al. (2013) worked at about 6 nm because neighbouring wavelengths are highly correlated. Here 5-nm averages are used for the searches, and indices and the red-edge position keep 1-nm precision.

The contact probe has its own lamp and no atmospheric path, so the water regions measure leaf water, which white rust reduces. Papers that removed them measured through the atmosphere (Mandal et al., 2023).

blocks.q: Why add wavelet and continuum-removal features to the DT-EDNet steps?
blocks.a: Ma et al. (2026) used image texture as a third feature family; single-leaf spectra have no texture. Wavelet features were the best single feature type for rice leaf blast (Tian et al., 2021) and southern corn leaf blight (Lv et al., 2023), and continuum-removal features were part of the powdery-mildew feature set of Zhang et al. (2012).

blocks.q: How do you make sure that feature selection did not see the test plots?
blocks.a: The whole chain is repeated on the training plots (E2); inner validation is by plot (B2); scaling is fitted inside each fold (E3); the test plots are opened once (F).
They were exact copies of other leaf columns of the same plot and date (13 March 2026); identical spectra cannot come from two leaves, so keeping them would count the same leaf twice.

blocks.q: Why are the networks trained for 100 and not 300 epochs?
blocks.a: Training on CPU; the patience (20 of 100) keeps the same ratio as Ma et al. (2026) (60 of 300), and early stopping keeps the best epoch.

blocks.q: Why judge the spectra against a model without sensors?
blocks.a: Severity follows crop age and date; weather-based models predict disease (Chattopadhyay et al., 2011; Bhattacharya and Chattopadhyay, 2013). The spectra are credited only with what they add (Zhang et al., 2014a).

blocks.q: Which metric is the main one?
blocks.a: Macro-F1 for detection and grades (Ma et al., 2026; Lv et al., 2023), because the classes are unequal; QWK for the order of the grades; R², RMSE and RPD for the score (Mandal et al., 2023).
